extracted.intended_audience: litigators, judges, and legal counsel handling equitable relief and unfair-competition disputes (news agency context)
extracted.subtask_description: A court brief arguing entitlement to (or opposing) a preliminary injunction in an unfair-competition suit between news-distributing agencies, focusing on equitable defenses (e.g., unclean hands), property rights in news, and the permissible use of competitors' published items as 'tips'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unauthorized agent acts do not bar equitable relief ('unclean hands')
rubrics_metrics.description: The unauthorized act of an agent cannot convict the principal of 'unclean hands' so as to bar the principal from equitable relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites authority (Vulcan Detinning Co. v. American Can Co.). Even if an agent is guilty, that guilt will not be imputed to the principal so as to deprive the principal of equitable remedies unless the requisite legal standard for imputation is met. The brief emphasizes that imputation for legal rights is distinct from moral standing: the principal's conscience may be void of offence though legal rights are determined with reference to imputed knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: To invoke 'unclean hands' defendant must show policy-level approval of unlawful practices
rubrics_metrics.description: To bar the complainant from relief, defendant must show not only an unlawful or surreptitious practice by complainant's agents, but that such practice has the knowledge and approval of those responsible for the complainant's policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Isolated or sporadic instances by minor employees are insufficient. The defense requires proof of a general practice known to and approved by management (those responsible for policies). The brief repeatedly stresses that 'a showing of a general practice could not suffice, unless it were known or approved by those responsible for the complainant's policies.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Respondeat superior may impute agent guilt to a defendant for injunction purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: When the defendant stands in the position of a principal, the doctrine of respondeat superior applies in all of its legal effects; the guilt of an agent unknown to the principal may render the defendant subject to injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts complainant's situation (where unauthorized agent acts don't bar relief) with defendant's relation, where respondeat superior can make the defendant liable and subject to injunction even if officers did not know of the acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolated incidents do not establish an 'unclean hands' practice
rubrics_metrics.description: A few scattering, sporadic instances, even if true, do not prove a practice sufficient to establish 'unclean hands' and will not suffice to bar equitable relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The brief notes that defendant's affidavits contain mostly hazy, indefinite charges and only a few specific instances; such evidence fails to show facts from which any inference of an established unlawful practice can be drawn. The criterion requires practice/policy-level sanction, not sporadic acts or confused recollections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between permissible 'tip' use and impermissible appropriation/resale
rubrics_metrics.description: Two uses of news from newspapers are distinguished: (1) using published news as a 'tip' to prompt independent, costly investigation and then distributing an independently gathered story (historically accepted), and (2) sending out a story based wholly or partly based on the rival's newspaper item without independent investigation (unfair and not permitted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'tip' is used as a suggestion for investigation; the resulting dispatch is the product of the recipient's own independent effort and expense and thus not appropriative. By contrast, appropriation/resale (textual or paraphrased) is described as unfair competition: it appropriates another's product at trivial cost, allows underselling, and may involve misrepresentation of authorship or service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriation/resale constitutes unfair competition (harm factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriating and reselling another news organization's dispatches (textually or paraphrased) is unfair competition because it permits the appropriator to undersell the original producer and to misrepresent the origin of the news to readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The brief explains two harms: (1) economic — a competitor can undersell by appropriating a story produced at large expense for a trivial cost; (2) reputational/misrepresentation — publishing the item as the defendant's own report or as Associated Press news falsely implies independent service or access. These harms justify injunctive relief against appropriation/resale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common consent and evolving business conditions affect fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: The fairness of practices (e.g., using newspaper items as 'tips') depends on prevailing business conditions and mutual acceptance; practices once fair may become unfair as the industry evolves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The brief acknowledges that the practice of 'tipping' has 'generally obtained with all of the news-gathering organizations' and that whether it is 'unjust or unlawful or constitutes unfair competition is perhaps a question.' It also states willingness to discontinue the practice if court finds it unfair, and observes that law of unfair competition changes with business developments (telegraph, wireless).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible scope of injunction (tailored relief)
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction should be limited to prevent appropriation and resale of published news items (textual or paraphrased), while not necessarily prohibiting the use of published items solely as rumors subject to independent and costly investigation — unless the Court finds even that practice unfair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The brief requests an injunction 'as to published news items' only 'against their appropriation and resale either in textual or paraphrased form and not against the use of such published news items solely as rumors' used for independent investigation. It offers to cease the tipping practice if the Court deems it unfair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for granting preliminary injunction in this context
rubrics_metrics.description: Complainant is entitled to a preliminary injunction where there is sufficient showing on confidential relations, breach of contract, or unfair competition; even if legal doubt exists, injunction may be granted pending final determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paragraphs (a), (c), and (d) of the prayer cover confidential relation and breach of contract (defendant concedes law and has admitted enough facts to justify injunction). Paragraph (e) covers unfair competition. The brief cites authorities to support that injunctions may be issued pendente lite pending final hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence quality: positive, first-hand affidavits vs. vague recollections
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits based on positive, personal knowledge by men in all branches of the service that a practice is forbidden are stronger evidence than hazy, indefinite recollections or the 'lapse of time' defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The brief contrasts the complainant's numerous rebutting affidavits by operators and managers who 'state in the most positive terms' that forbidden practices never occurred, with defendant's affiants whose memories are 'hazy' or confused. It uses this to argue insufficiency of defendant's claims to establish a systemic wrongful practice.
